paragraphs.text: SERIES A.
I. HERE BEGINS THE CATHOLIC FAITH SET FORTH AT THE CITY OF PARIS BY THE BISHOPS OF GAUL TO THE EASTERN BISHOPS.
The bishops of Gaul send greetings to their most beloved and most blessed fellow priests, all the Eastern bishops who abide in Christ throughout the various provinces.

With every sense of our life and faith we give thanks to God the Father through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through the teachings of the prophets and apostles he has set us in the light of the knowledge of confessing him, so that we are not held in the darkness of worldly ignorance and bound by the judgment of the world. For the one and fullest hope of salvation is to confess God the Father almighty through his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, in the Holy Spirit.

But plainly no smaller cause for our rejoicing grows each day: having freed us from the error of the world, he now also does not allow us to be mixed into the inexpiable fellowship of heretics. For from your letter, which you entrusted to our beloved brother and fellow priest Hilary, we have learned of the devil's deceit and of the schemes of heretics conspiring against the Lord's church. Their aim was that we should be divided between East and West and misled by opinions that differed from one another.

For a great many of those who were present at Rimini or at Nike were forced, under the authority of your name, to keep silent about "ousia". That word was once found by you against the heresy of the Ariomaniacs, and we have always received it in holiness and faith.

For we have embraced the word "homoousion" to express the true and legitimate birth of the only-begotten God from God the Father. We detest the idea of a single union in the manner of Sabellius's blasphemies. Nor do we understand the Son to be some part of the Father. Rather, we understand that the whole and perfect only-begotten God was born from the whole and perfect unbegotten God. For that reason we confess him to be of "one" "ousia" or "substance" with God the Father, so that he may not be thought instead to be a creature, or an adopted son, or a son in name only. And because he is from him, as Son from Father, God from God, power from power, spirit from spirit, light from light, we are not unwilling to hear of his likeness to God the Father, since he is indeed the image of the invisible God. But we understand the only likeness worthy of the Father to be that of true God to true God. In this way what is understood is not a union of the Godhead but a unity, because a union is singular, while a unity, according to the truth of the birth, is the fullness of the one who is born,

especially since the Lord Jesus Christ himself declared to his disciples: "I and the Father are one." By this he signifies not only the love he bears toward the Father but also the divinity that belongs to God from God. This agrees with the sayings "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father too" and "If you will not believe me, at least believe my works, for the Father is in me and I am in the Father."

We have always held this faith and will go on holding it. We also detest those who say, "He did not exist before he was born." We do not preach that the only-begotten God is unbegotten. But it is supremely impious to place any time before God, the God of all times, since the very statement "before he was born, he did not exist" belongs to time.

Nor do we deny that he was obedient to the Father, even to the point of death on the cross, according to the weakness of the manhood he assumed. For he himself said of his ascent to heaven: "If you loved me, you would rejoice, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I." By taking flesh he deigned to call us his brothers, since, while remaining in the form of God, he willed to be in the form of a servant.

So, dearest brothers, from your letter our simplicity now recognizes that it was deceived over the silence about "ousia". As the contents of your letter testify, your piety met with those who returned from Rimini to Constantinople. Our brother Hilary, the faithful preacher of the Lord's name, has reported that you could not compel them to condemn such great blasphemies. We too therefore withdraw from everything that was wrongly done through ignorance.

In accordance with your letter, we hold Auxentius, Ursacius and Valens, Gaius, Megasius and Justin to be excommunicated. As we have said, this also certainly agrees with the declaration of our brother Hilary, who stated that he would not be at peace with those who followed their errors. All the blasphemies as well

which you appended to your letter we condemn. Above all we reject their apostate priests, who were most unworthily put in the places of brothers now in exile, through either the ignorance or the impiety of certain people. We promise this before God, and we also declare that anyone within the Gallic provinces who decides to resist what we have decreed is to be cast out of communion and out of his priestly see. For no one will be judged worthy of the holiness of the priestly name who, as in other matters, either allows an opportunity to preach what we do not condemn [?], or strives against God and the majesty of Christ, the only-begotten God, by thinking otherwise than we do about the meaning of "homoousion".

Your charity should know that Saturninus, who most impiously opposed these salutary decrees, has already been excommunicated from the priesthood by all the bishops of Gaul, in accordance with the two letters of our brothers. His old crimes, long concealed though they were, together with the sure evidence of his new recklessness published in his letters, have made him unworthy of the name of bishop.
HERE ENDS THE CATHOLIC FAITH SET FORTH AT THE CITY OF PARIS BY THE BISHOPS OF GAUL TO THE EASTERN BISHOPS.
II. Eusebius sends greetings in the Lord to his most holy lord and brother, Bishop Gregory.

(5). I have received your Sincerity's letter. From it I learned that, as befits a bishop and priest of God, you resisted the transgressor Ossius. When very many at Rimini fell into communion with Valens, Ursacius and the rest, whom they themselves had earlier condemned once they recognized their crime of blasphemy, you refused your assent and kept the faith that the fathers of Nicaea wrote down. We congratulate you on this, and we congratulate ourselves as well, because you live by this resolve and, strong in this faith, have deigned to remember us.

As long as you remain in the same confession and keep no fellowship with hypocrites, you may count on our communion with you. With whatever treatises you can and with all the effort you can manage, reprove the transgressors and rebuke the unbelievers. Fear nothing from the worldly kingdom, as you have done so far, for the one who is in us is greater than the one who is in this world.

We, your fellow priests, who are enduring a third exile, say what we have taken to be plain: the whole hope of the Ariomaniacs rests not on their own agreement, which is hardly united, but on the protection of the worldly kingdom. They do not know the scripture which says that those who put their hope in man are cursed. But our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth. We wish to endure in our sufferings, so that, as it is said, we may be glorified in the kingdom.

Please write and tell us what progress you have made in correcting the wicked, and how many brothers you have found standing firm or have yourself corrected by your admonitions. All who are with me send you greetings, especially the deacon. Together they ask that you kindly greet with our respects all those who faithfully stand by your side.
HERE ENDS THE LETTER OF EUSEBIUS TO GREGORY, BISHOP IN SPAIN.
III. HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF BISHOP GERMINIUS AGAINST THE ARIANS,
WHO HAD ALREADY SIGNED AT THE COUNCIL OF RIMINI, KNOWING THAT THEY HAD DONE WRONG.
I, Bishop Germinius, believe and profess that there is one true God the Father, eternal and almighty,

and Christ his only Son, our Lord and God, true Son of God from the true God the Father, begotten before all things. He is like the Father in all things: in divinity, love, majesty, power, glory, life, wisdom and knowledge, since he is perfect, begotten from one who is perfect.

We also accept and believe that he took up manhood from the Virgin Mary, as the prophets foretold would happen and as the voices of the Gospels and the apostles teach was fulfilled. We likewise accept and believe his passion, death, resurrection and ascension into heaven. And we profess that at the end of the world he will come down from heaven

to judge the living and the dead and to repay each person according to his works. And we believe in the Holy Spirit, that is, the Paraclete, who has been given to us by God the Father through the Son.
IV.
HERE BEGINS THE DECREE OF THE SYNOD OF THE EASTERN BISHOPS OF THE ARIAN PARTY AT SERDICA, WHICH THEY SENT TO AFRICA.

To Gregory, bishop of Alexandria; to the bishop of Nicomedia; to the bishop of Carthage; to a bishop of Campania; to the bishop of Naples in Campania; to the clergy of Rimini; to a bishop of Campania; to the bishop of Salona in Dalmatia; to Amphion, Donatus, Desiderius, Fortunatus, Eutychius, Maximus, Sympheron; and to all our fellow priests throughout the world, the presbyters and deacons, and all who are in the holy catholic church under heaven. We bishops, who gathered from various provinces of the East and held a council at the city of Serdica, send eternal salvation in the Lord. We came from the province of the Thebaid and the province of Palestine, and from Arabia, Phoenicia, Syria, Mesopotamia, Cilicia, [Galatia], Isauria, Cappadocia, Galatia, Pontus, Bithynia, Pamphylia, Paphlagonia, Caria, Phrygia, Pisidia, the islands of the Cyclades, Lydia, Asia, Europa, the Hellespont, Thrace and Haemimontus.

Our prayer never fails, dearly beloved brothers. First, we pray that the holy and catholic church of the Lord may be free of all dissensions and schisms and may everywhere preserve the unity of the Spirit and the bond of love through right faith. It is indeed right for all who call on the Lord to hold, embrace, guard and keep a spotless life as well, and above all for us bishops who preside over the most holy churches. Second, we pray that the church's rule and the holy tradition and judgments of the fathers may remain firm and solid forever. May they never be disturbed by new sects and perverse traditions as they spring up, especially in the appointing and deposing of bishops, so that the church does not fail to keep the gospel and the holy precepts. These are what were commanded to the holy and most blessed apostles, and they have been kept by our forebears and by ourselves to this day, and are still kept.

For in our times there has arisen a certain Marcellus of Galatia, the most accursed plague of all the heretics. With a sacrilegious mind, a profane mouth and a depraved argument, he seeks to set limits to the perpetual, eternal and timeless kingdom of Christ the Lord. He says that the Lord received the beginning of his reign four hundred years ago and that it will come to an end together with the passing away of the world.
With reckless boldness he even tries to assert that at the conception of his body he was then made

the image of the invisible God, and that only then did he become bread, door and life. He maintains this not only in words and in talkative assertions. He has also put everything that he conceived with a sacrilegious mind and uttered with a blasphemous mouth into a book, driven by eager desire, a book full of blasphemies and abominations. In it he has added other things far worse, slandering him by means of the divine scriptures through his own interpretation and wicked mind, applying them in a sense contrary to their meaning out of his pestilent understanding.

From these things it is clearly and plainly established that he is a heretic. He mixes his assertions with filth of various kinds: now with the falsehoods of Sabellius, now with the malice of Paul of Samosata, now openly with the blasphemies of Montanus, the leader of all heretics. He makes a single confusion out of all these, and like a foolish Galatian he has turned aside to another gospel, which is not another. As the blessed apostle Paul says in condemning such people: "Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you anything other than what you have received, let him be anathema."
Our fathers and forebears were greatly concerned about this sacrilegious preaching. For a council of bishops was summoned to

the city of Constantinople, in the presence of the emperor Constantine of most blessed memory. Bishops came from many provinces of the East to reform, by wholesome counsel, a man steeped in evil, so that he might be corrected by admonition and most holy reproof and abandon his sacrilegious preaching. For a long time they rebuked him, reproached him, and even pleaded with him in loving affection, but they achieved nothing.

After a first and a second and many reproofs they still could achieve nothing, for he persisted, contradicted the right faith, and resisted the catholic church with malicious contentiousness. From then on everyone began to shudder at him and avoid him. Seeing that he was perverted, that he was sinning, and that he stood condemned by his own judgment, they condemned him in ecclesiastical acts, so that he could no longer defile the sheep of Christ with his evil and pestilent contact. At that time they also deposited some of his most depraved opinions against the right faith and the most holy church in the church's archive, together with their own most holy writings, as a record and a warning for those who come after.

These were only the first things in the impiety of Marcellus the heretic; worse things followed. For who among the faithful could believe or tolerate what he wickedly did and wrote? These things had already been deservedly anathematized, together with Marcellus himself, by our fathers in the city of Constantinople. For there exists a book of sentences written against him by the bishops. In that book even those who are now with Marcellus and support him, namely Protogenes, bishop of the city of Serdica, and Cyriacus of Naissus, wrote out the sentence against him with their own hands. Their own valid signature testifies that the most holy faith must in no way be changed, and that the holy church must not be overturned by false preaching. Otherwise a most grievous plague and pestilence of souls would be brought upon people, as Paul says: "Whether we or an angel from heaven should preach to you anything other than what you have received, let him be anathema."

But we were greatly astonished that certain men who wish to be regarded as churchmen readily receive into communion someone who dares to preach a gospel other than the true one. They do not examine his blasphemies, which are recorded in his own book,

and they have refused to agree with those who investigated everything carefully and, once they found these blasphemies, justly condemned him. For since Marcellus was regarded as a heretic among his own people, he sought the help that travel abroad could give him, so that he might deceive those who did not know him or his pestilent writings. But whatever he does among them, he conceals his impious writings and profane opinions and puts forward falsehoods in place of the truth, and so he has made a profit out of the simple and innocent. Under the pretext of the church's rule he has led many shepherds of the church astray and brought them under his power. Introducing the sect of the heretic Sabellius, he has deceived them with cunning fraud and revived the arts and tricks of Paul of Samosata.

For, as was said above, the alien tradition of Marcellus is mixed with the sects of all the heretics. So all who preside over the holy church should have remembered the words of Christ the Lord, who says: "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. By their fruits you will know them." They ought to have avoided such men, shuddered at them, and not readily held communion with them,

but recognized them by their deeds and condemned them in advance on the basis of their sacrilegious writings. But now we greatly fear that in our own times what is written may be fulfilled: "While people were sleeping, the enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat." For when those who ought to keep watch in guarding the church do not keep watch, falsehoods that imitate the truth overturn what is right from its very foundations.

We, then, have fully learned of Marcellus's sect and his crimes from his own book. We have therefore written to you, dearly beloved brothers, so that you will not admit to the communion of the holy church either Marcellus or those who join him. Remember the prophet David, who says: "I said to those who do wickedness, 'Do not do wickedness,' and to the sinners, 'Do not lift up the horn; do not lift your horn on high; do not speak injustice against God.'" And believe Solomon, who says: "Do not move the eternal boundary stones that your fathers set up."

Since this is so, do not follow the errors of the most depraved Marcellus mentioned above. Condemn in advance what he devised and handed down against Christ the Lord in his unjust preaching, so that you do not also become sharers in his blasphemies and crimes. But for brevity's sake, so much for Marcellus.

Now hear what was done concerning Athanasius, formerly bishop of Alexandria. He was gravely accused of being sacrilegious toward God and profane toward the mysteries of the holy church. With his own hands he smashed the chalice dedicated to God and Christ, broke the venerable altar itself, overturned the priestly chair, and himself demolished to the ground the very basilica, the house of God, the church of Christ. As for the presbyter himself, a serious and upright man named Ischyras, he handed him over to military custody.

He was also accused of assaults, violence, murder and the outright slaughter of bishops. Even during the most holy days of Easter he raged like a tyrant, in league with the generals and counts. On his account they shut some people up in prison, tormented others with blows and scourges, and forced the rest into his sacrilegious communion by various tortures. Such acts had never been committed by the innocent. By these means he hoped that his followers and his faction could prevail. Through generals and judges, through prisons, blows and various tortures, he would compel the unwilling into his communion, force those who refused, and terrorize like a tyrant those who opposed and resisted him. Serious and bitter indeed were the charges his accusers brought against him.
Because of these things a council was of necessity first summoned at Caesarea in Palestine. When neither he nor his henchmen came to that council,

another was of necessity held a year later at Tyre because of his crimes. Bishops came from Macedonia, Pannonia, Bithynia and all parts of the East, obliged to attend by the emperor's command. When they learned of Athanasius's outrages and crimes from the records, they did not believe the accusers indiscriminately or rashly. Instead they chose distinguished and praiseworthy bishops from their council and sent them to the very place where the deeds of which Athanasius was accused had taken place. These bishops saw everything with their own eyes and learned the truth.

Then they returned to the council and by their testimony confirmed that the crimes alleged by the accusers were true. So, in Athanasius's presence, the council pronounced a sentence worthy of his crimes. For this reason he fled from Tyre and appealed to the emperor. The emperor also heard the case. After holding an inquiry he recognized all his outrages and by his own sentence deported him into exile. Matters having turned out this way, Athanasius was rightly condemned and held in exile as his crimes deserved: sacrilegious toward God, profane toward the sacred mysteries, violent in demolishing a basilica, horrifying in the deaths of bishops and the persecution of innocent brothers. In rejecting evildoers, all the bishops upheld the authority of the law, the canon of the church and the holy tradition of the apostles.
But Athanasius, after his condemnation, contrived his return from exile, and after a very long time he came from Gaul to Alexandria.

Treating his past deeds as nothing, he grew still more powerful in wickedness. For compared with what followed, his first offenses were slight. All along the route of his return he overturned churches. He restored some condemned bishops and held out to others the hope of returning to their sees. Some he made bishops from among unbelievers, through brawls and killings by pagans, while sound priests were still alive and in office. He had no regard for the laws and gave himself over wholly to desperate measures.

So by force, by slaughter and by war he plundered the basilicas of the Alexandrians. A holy and sound priest had already been installed in his place by the judgment of the council. Yet like a barbarian enemy, like a sacrilegious plague, he brought in crowds of pagans, burned the temple of God and smashed the altar. Then he slipped out of the city secretly and fled into hiding.

As for Paul, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, anyone who hears what he did after his return from exile will shudder. [?] At Ancyra too, in the province of Galatia, after the return of the heretic Marcellus there were houses set on fire and fighting of every kind. He had presbyters dragged naked to the forum. And, what must be told with tears and grief, he openly and publicly profaned the consecrated body of the Lord, which had been hung around the necks of the priests. Most holy virgins dedicated to God and Christ he publicly stripped of their clothing and exposed naked, with horrifying shamelessness, in the forum in the middle of the city, while crowds gathered.

In the city of Gaza in the province of Palestine, too, Asclepas smashed the altar after his return and stirred up many riots. Moreover, at Adrianople Lucius, after his return, ordered that the sacrifice consecrated by holy and sound priests be thrown, if one may even say it, to the dogs. Since this is how things stand, are we still to entrust the sheep of Christ to wolves so many and so savage, and make the members of Christ the members of a harlot? Far from it!

Afterwards Athanasius travelled through various parts of the world. He led some astray and deceived innocent bishops who knew nothing of his crimes with his trickery and poisonous flattery, or he begged written testimonials from individual Egyptians who knew nothing of his conduct. In this way he threw peaceful churches into turmoil, or else he forged new letters for himself as he pleased. Yet none of this could prevail against the judgment that had long since been solemnly pronounced by most holy and distinguished bishops. For the commendation of men who were not judges at the council, who never had the council's judgment in their hands, and who are known not even to have been present

when the aforesaid Athanasius was given his hearing could neither help nor benefit him. Finally, when he realized that these efforts had come to nothing, he went to Julius at Rome, and also to certain bishops of his own party. He deceived them with forged letters, and they very readily received him into communion. From then on they began to labour not so much for him as for their own conduct, because they had believed him far too rashly and entered into communion with him. Even if those letters did come from certain people, they did not come from those who had been judges or had sat in the council. And even if they had come from such people, these bishops ought never to have rashly trusted a man pleading his own cause.

But they refused to believe the judges who had justly sentenced him. (11) The reason is this: others who in the past were also exposed for their crimes are now joined with Marcellus and Athanasius. We mean Asclepas, who was stripped of the episcopal dignity seventeen years ago, then Paul and Lucius and all who have joined such men. Going round foreign regions together, they persuaded judges that those who had

justly pronounced sentence against them were not to be believed, so that by this kind of trafficking they might one day secure their return to their sees. They did not defend themselves in the very places where they had sinned, nor in neighbouring places, nor where they had accusers. Instead they went to strangers who lived far from their own regions and did not know the truth of what had happened. Before them they tried to break a just sentence, laying their conduct before people who knew nothing whatever about it. They do this cunningly.

They knew that many of the judges, accusers and witnesses had died after so many and such weighty sentences. So they thought to set up a new trial, wishing to plead their case before us, who neither acquitted them nor judged them. For those who did judge them have already gone to the Lord.

They also wished, in the case of the Eastern bishops [?], that defenders should come in place of judges, and in place of defenders [?]. This was at a time when their defence carried no weight, above all because they could by no means defend themselves back when their accusers confronted them face to face.

They thought to introduce a new law, that Eastern bishops should be judged by Western ones. And they wanted the church's judgment to rest with men who cared less for the accused than for their own conduct. Since church discipline has never admitted such wickedness, we ask you, dearest brothers, to join us in condemning the criminal ruin and deadly schemes of these lost men.

For while Athanasius was still a bishop, he himself condemned the deposed Asclepas by his own sentence. Marcellus too never communicated with him. Paul, moreover, was present at the deposition of Athanasius, wrote out the sentence with his own hand, and with the others condemned him himself. And as long as each of them was a bishop, he upheld his own judgments.

But when, for different reasons and at different times, each of them was justly driven out of the church as he deserved, they formed a greater concord through a single conspiracy. Each of them pardoned the others the offences which they had condemned with divine authority while they were bishops.

Athanasius went to Italy and Gaul and procured a trial for himself after the death of some of the accusers, witnesses and judges. He believed that he could be heard anew at a time when his outrages would be obscured by the passage of time. Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, Maximinus, Ossius and many others wrongly gave him their support, and through the emperors' kindness obtained permission for their council to be held at Serdica.

Summoned by the emperor's letters, we hastened to Serdica. When we arrived, we learned that Athanasius, Marcellus and all the criminals who had been driven out by the sentence of a council, and each justly condemned for his crimes,

were sitting in the middle of the church with Ossius and Protogenes, debating together and, worse still, celebrating the divine mysteries. Nor was Protogenes, bishop of Serdica, ashamed to communicate with the heretic Marcellus. In council he had himself condemned with his own voice both Marcellus's sect and his reprobate opinions, subscribing four times to the sentences of the bishops. It is clear, then, that he condemned himself by his own sentence when he made himself Marcellus's partner by communicating with him.

We, however, held to the discipline of the church's rule and wished to help these wretched men a little. So we instructed those who were with Protogenes and Ossius to exclude the condemned from their assembly and not to communicate with sinners, and then to hear together with us

what our fathers had decided against these men in the past. Marcellus's book needed no accuser, for it showed him plainly to be a heretic. And so that they would not be swayed by false insinuations, none of them was to cloak a thoroughly depraved mind behind the rank of bishop. But they resisted this, for what reason we do not know. They refused to separate themselves from communion with these men. By upholding the sect of the heretic Marcellus, they set the crimes of Athanasius and the misdeeds of the others above the faith and peace of the church.

When we learned this, we eighty bishops, who had come to Serdica from various distant provinces at great cost and labour to strengthen the peace of the church, saw it and could not bear it without tears. It was no light matter that they flatly refused to dismiss from their company those whom our fathers had previously and justly condemned for their crimes.

So we judged it wicked to communicate with them. We would not mingle the Lord's holy sacraments with profane men, for we kept and held to the discipline of the church's rule. Perhaps Ossius and Protogenes did not dismiss the aforesaid from their company because of a bad conscience: each of them feared being exposed by someone, and greatly dreaded having those things brought to light. Nor, for the same reason, did any of them dare pronounce sentence against these men. He would have condemned himself, since they had communicated, against the prohibition, with men with whom they ought by no means to communicate.

But we begged them again and again not to shake what is firm and solid, not to overturn the law or disturb divine ordinances, not to throw everything into confusion, and not to set aside even the smallest part of the church's tradition. We begged them not to introduce a new sect, and not to give those coming from the West precedence in any respect over the Eastern bishops and their most holy councils.

They, however, despised all this and threatened us, promising that they would vindicate Athanasius and the other criminals. As if they could do or say anything else, when they had taken all the criminals and lost men into their fellowship! Moreover, they put forward this claim with great arrogance, driven by audacity and rashness rather than by lawful reasoning. They saw that those who receive the condemned incur offence and guilt as violators of heavenly laws. So they tried to set up a tribunal with such authority that they could call themselves judges of the judges and, if that were lawful, reopen the sentence of men who are already with God.
For a great many days we begged them to cast off the condemned, to unite themselves to the holy church, and to agree with the fathers, who spoke the truth. But they flatly refused to do so.

While we were disputing, five bishops of our party came forward. They are the survivors of the six who had been sent to the Mareotis. They offered the others this proposal: that some bishops from each council should be sent to the places where Athanasius had committed his crimes and outrages, to write everything down faithfully with God as their witness. If what we had reported to the council should be found

false, we would be condemned and would not complain to the emperors, to the council, or to any bishop. But if what we had said before proved to be true, then, to match our number, we would depose those of you whom you chose [?], that is, those who communicated with Athanasius after his condemnation, as well as those who are supporters and defenders of Athanasius and Marcellus. And none of you would complain to the emperors, to the council, or to any bishop. Ossius and Protogenes and all their associates were afraid to accept this proposal put forward by our side.

Meanwhile, a vast crowd of every kind of criminal and lost man had poured into Serdica from Constantinople and from Alexandria. Among them were men guilty of murder, bloodshed, slaughter, robbery, plunder, looting and every unspeakable sacrilege and crime. They had smashed altars, burned churches and ransacked private houses. They had profaned God's mysteries and betrayed Christ's sacraments. Asserting the impious and wicked doctrine of the heretics against the church's

faith, they had savagely butchered God's wisest presbyters, deacons and bishops. Ossius and Protogenes had all these men gathered with them in their little conventicle. They honoured these men and despised all of us, God's deacons and bishops, because we would never consent to join with such men. These men also reported to the populace and to all the pagans what had passed among us, inventing falsehoods in place of the truth. They claimed that the discord had arisen not from God's cause but from human presumption.

Mixing human affairs with divine and joining private interests to the church's business, they stirred up an outcry and a riot in the city against us. They said that we had done the city grave injury by schism unless we communicated with them, which would have been a sin, and they shouted this over and over. For we utterly refused to communicate with them unless they cast out those whom we had condemned and paid due honour to the council of the East.

From what follows you will be able to learn what they did and what kind of council they held. Protogenes, as we said above, anathematized Marcellus and Paul in the official acts, yet afterwards received them into communion. And they had at their council Dionysius of Elis in the province of Achaea, whom they themselves had deposed. Deposers and deposed together, judges and defendants, sharing communion, they handle the divine mysteries.

They also ordained as bishop Bassus of the city of Diocletianopolis, who had been exposed in outrages and crimes and had justly been banished from Syria. He was then found living even more wickedly among them and was condemned by them, yet today he is plainly joined with them. As for Aetius of Thessalonica, Protogenes often hurled many reproaches and charges at him, saying that he had kept concubines and was still keeping them, and he never wanted to communicate with him. Now Aetius has been received into friendship, as if he had been cleansed by the company of worse men, and among them he is regarded as a righteous man.

Asclepas came to the city of Constantinople on Paul's account. There monstrous and atrocious deeds were committed in the middle of the church of Constantinople: a thousand murders that defiled the very altars with human blood, the slaughter of brethren and the deaths of pagans. Yet to this day he does not cease to communicate with Paul, for whose sake all this was done. The same is true of those who communicate with Paul through Asclepas, receiving letters from him and sending letters to him.

From such a clotted mass and gathering of lost men, what kind of council could be held? In it they did not so much punish their outrages as acknowledge them! (21) For it is not in our manner, we who preside over the most holy churches and are rulers

of the peoples, that they grant and remit what can never be remitted or granted by them. Indeed, they even pardoned Marcellus, Athanasius and the other criminals their outrages and blasphemy, which it was a sin to remit, even though it is written: "If a man sins against a man, they will pray to the Lord for him; but if a man sins against God, who will pray for him?"

We have no such custom, nor does the church of God. We do not allow anyone to teach such things or to introduce new traditions. Otherwise we would be called betrayers of the faith and surrenderers of the divine Scriptures, which is a sin, and we would be condemned by the Lord and by men.

The aforesaid men also devised the following schemes against us. They knew that we could not communicate with them as a favour to criminals, so they thought to frighten us with letters from the emperors and drag us into their communion against our will. And they were ready to watch the deep and lasting peace of the church throughout the world being divided for the sake of

Athanasius and Marcellus, through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed among the nations. If these two had any fear of God in them, they ought to have abandoned their utterly depraved presumption, even at this late hour. Then the disturbance they caused would not continue, and the church would not be divided against itself on their account. Or, if those who fight on their behalf had any fear of God, then even if nothing worthy of condemnation were found in these men, they ought still to curse and abhor them. For the unity of the church is being split because of them, and its deep peace is being overturned through mad rage and lust for honour.
When we saw how matters were going, each of us decided to return home. We resolved to write from Serdica, to report what had happened and to declare our sentence.

We cannot again receive into the honour of the episcopate Athanasius and Marcellus, who were deposed and condemned long ago. They lived as criminals, impiously blaspheming against the Lord. They crucified the Son of God afresh and, holding him up to public contempt once more, pierced him with cruel blows. One of them, by blaspheming against the Son of God and his kingdom, has died once and for all an eternal death. The other sinned atrociously and profanely against the body of the Lord and his mysteries, and committed other monstrous outrages, and he was cast out and condemned by the sentence of bishops.

We cannot depart from the tradition of our forefathers, because the church has never claimed such authority and has not received such power from God. For this reason we do not ourselves receive the aforesaid men back into the honour and dignity of the church, and we justly condemn those who do receive them.

Nor do we receive into the church others who have justly been condemned, whether long ago or more recently. We adhere to the laws of God, the traditions of the fathers and the discipline of the church, and we believe the prophet who says: "Do not move the ancient boundaries which your fathers set." Therefore we never shake what is fixed and solid, but rather preserve what was established by our forefathers.

After much has been said, then, dearest brothers, we give you this instruction openly. Let none of you, deceived by anyone, ever communicate with Ossius, Protogenes, Athanasius, Marcellus, Asclepas, Paul or Julius. Do not communicate with any of the condemned who have been cast out of the holy church, nor with their associates who communicate with them, whether in person or by letter. You must therefore never write to them nor receive letters from them. As for what remains,

we beg you, dearest brothers, to look to the unity of the church and to lasting peace, and to choose holy bishops whose faith is sound and whose life is holy. Shun those who have been stripped of the episcopal honour for their crimes

and who wish to recover the place they justly lost through their misdeeds. Curse ever more strongly those whom you see committing worse things after their crime, and who do not listen to the Lord when he says: "You have sinned; be still." For such men grow young again and become stronger through their crimes. The deeper they sink into the whirlpool of vice, the more they overturn the whole world. Through their vicious seditions they bring wars and the fiercest persecutions upon the holy churches, and like tyrants they strive to take the peoples of God captive under their own rule.

Recognize their utterly wicked aims from what has happened. They have unleashed such a storm on the world that it has thrown almost the whole East and West into turmoil. Each of us had to leave the care of our churches, desert the peoples of God, set aside the very teaching of the gospel and come from far away: old men weighed down by age, weak in body and infirm with sickness. We were dragged from place to place and had to leave our sick companions behind on the road, all because of a handful of criminals justly condemned long ago, who are seeking the primacy of the church against all right. Meanwhile the imperial government has to concern itself with us, and religious emperors, tribunes and generals are kept busy over the life and standing of bishops, to the grievous harm of the commonwealth [?]. Nor are the peoples silent. The whole brotherhood in every province waits in suspense and anxiety to see how this storm of evils will end.

Even the public post is worn out and reduced to nothing. Why say more? The East and West of the world are being overturned from their foundations and thrown into turmoil by a harsh and savage storm, all because of one or two or a few criminals who think impiously and live shamefully, men in whom no seed of religion has taken root. If they had any, they would imitate the prophet who says: "Pick me up and throw me into the sea, and the sea will become calm for you, for this storm has come because of me." But they do not imitate him, because they do not follow the righteous either. Thus the ringleaders of all the criminals seek the leadership of the church as if it were a tyrant's kingdom.

Nor do they seek this out of any concern for goodness or justice. Men who try to dissolve the laws, the divine ordinances and the decrees of others do not care for the churches. That is why they were trying to introduce this novelty, which the ancient custom of the church abhors: that whatever the Eastern bishops might have decided in council should be reopened by the Western bishops, and likewise that whatever the bishops of the Western regions decided should be undone by the Eastern ones. But they were pursuing this out of that utterly depraved mind of theirs.

On the contrary, the acts of our ancestors attest that the decrees of all councils justly and lawfully conducted are to be upheld. The council held in the city of Rome concerning the heretics Novatus, Sabellius and Valentinus was confirmed by the Easterners. And again, what was decreed in the East concerning Paul of Samosata was signed by everyone.

We therefore urge you, dearest brothers, to consider the order of church discipline and to have regard for the peace of the whole world. Rebuke those who communicate with criminals, and cut the wicked out of the churches root and branch. Then, as the storm they have caused rages, Christ the Lord, walking upon the waters, may command all the winds and storms of the sea to depart, and grant the holy church lasting peace and quiet.

We, however, have done no one any wrong; we keep the precepts of the law. For we have been gravely wronged and badly treated by those who wanted to throw the rule of the catholic church into confusion through their depravity. But, keeping the fear of God before our eyes and considering the true and just judgment of Christ, we have shown partiality to no one, nor have we spared anyone in a way that would keep us from upholding the discipline of the church.

For this reason the whole council has condemned Julius of the city of Rome, Ossius, Protogenes, Gaudentius and Maximinus of Trier, in accordance with the most ancient law, as the authors of communion with Marcellus, Athanasius and the rest of the crim-

-inals, and as men who also shared in communion with the murders of Paul of Constantinople and his bloody deeds. Protogenes is to be anathematized together with Marcellus, since he frequently subscribed to the sentence passed against Marcellus himself and against his book. These men also passed sentence against

Paul of Constantinople and later entered into communion with him. Gaudentius is condemned for being unmindful of his predecessor Cyriacus, who subscribed to the sentences justly passed against the criminals, and for having involved himself in the crimes of Paul, whom he even shamelessly defended.

Julius of the city of Rome is condemned as the chief and leader of these evils. He was the first to open the door of communion to criminals and condemned men, and he made a way for the rest to dissolve the divine laws. He also defended

Athanasius presumptuously and boldly, a man whose witnesses and accusers alike he did not know. Ossius is condemned for the reason given above, and on account of Mark of most blessed memory, on whom he constantly inflicted grave injuries. He is also condemned because he defended with all his might all the wicked men justly condemned for their crimes, and because he lived in the East in the company of criminals and reprobates. He was shamefully the inseparable friend of Paulinus, formerly bishop of Dacia. That man was first accused of sorcery and expelled from the church, and to this day he remains in apostasy and openly fornicates with concubines and prostitutes. Macedonius of Mopsuestia, bishop and confessor, burned his books of sorcery. Ossius also clung most wickedly to Eustathius and Cymatius and was dear to them. Nothing need be said of their infamous and shameful lives, since their end has made them known to all. Joined from the beginning to these men and others like them, Ossius,

always fostering criminals, set himself against the church and always brought help to the enemies of God. Maximinus of Trier is condemned because he refused to receive our colleagues, the bishops whom we had sent to Gaul, and because he was the first to enter into communion with Paul of Constantinople, a wicked and abandoned man. He was also himself the cause of so great a disaster, namely that Paul was recalled to the city of Constantinople, and on Paul's account many murders were committed. So the man who recalled Paul to Constantinople after he had once been condemned was himself the cause of all those murders.

For these reasons, then, the council judged it just to cut off and condemn Julius of the city of Rome, Ossius and the others mentioned above. Since this is so, dearest brothers, you must guard yourselves against them and keep away from them. Never admit them to your communion, do not accept their letters, and do not send them letters of the Lord's fellowship [?].

And since Ossius' followers wanted to break down the catholic and apostolic faith by introducing the new, Judaizing sect of Marcellus, allied with the Jew [?] and mixed with Sabellius and Paul, we have necessarily set out the faith of the catholic church. Ossius' followers mentioned above have denied this faith and brought in the faith of the heretic Marcellus.
It follows that, once you have received our letter, each of you should give consent to this sentence and seal our decrees with your own signature.

To our lord Constantius Augustus, deservedly most glorious and most victorious, from the synod of Rimini, in agreement with the Easterners [that is, Migdonius, Megasius, Valens, Epictetus and the others who consented to the heresy].

Enlightened by your piety's letter, we have given and still give the greatest thanks to God that you have blessed us by informing us of what we ought to do in keeping with your piety's deliberation: that no one should use the names 'ousia' or 'homoousios', which were at one time unknown to the church of God and tend to cause scandal among brothers. We rejoiced greatly, because we recognized in this what we ourselves held.

O how blessed we are, to whom such great happiness has come! Through your piety's understanding, the others, who are accustomed to apply these names to God and the Son of God, have been refuted and have been given a limit. We therefore render obedience to your clemency, because the state of the truth has shone forth openly. Since truth cannot be conquered, it has also won the victory, so that a name unworthy of God, written nowhere in the holy laws, is now used by no one.

We therefore pray your piety, since we are still detained in the place where the synod was held and from which we gave our response through our envoys, to order that we, who hold the doctrine intact together with the Easterners, now be released to our peoples. In this way the lovers of truth, who do not change the name used of God, will be made plain, and we who hold the catholic truth will no longer be detained with those infected by perverse doctrine.

We therefore earnestly pray your piety, lord, before God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, God and Son of God, that you make us [?], who under your rule have subscribed to sound doctrine and withdrawn from the name 'ousia', (and) that you order us to be released to our peoples. Then the church, which does not in any way permit the names of God and his Son to be changed, may rejoice by command of your power and glory. On that power the Divinity has bestowed so much that, now that the sacrilege of the expression has become plain, the names 'ousia' and 'homoousios', which are not found written of God and the Son of God in the divine Scriptures, are now withdrawn.

Help, pious emperor, the worshippers of the most high God. Help those who pray to God the Father almighty through Christ the Son of God. Help those who offer devoted ears to your judgment, who know how to worship none but God the Father, through our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of his glory. And command, lord emperor, that we return to our peoples, by giving letters to Taurus, the most distinguished praetorian prefect, because

we too render full obedience to the Easterners and to your arrangement in proclaiming the name of God. In this matter, which we have always held, we ought now to return to our peoples. We have sent letters about this to our fellow bishops of the East, so that they may know that we have always held this and that we remain with them in the catholic faith. VII. HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF THE ENVOYS, SENT TO THE EMPEROR CONSTANTIUS BY LIBERIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME, THROUGH BISHOP LUCIFER.
To the most glorious Constantius Augustus, from Bishop Liberius.

I beseech you, most tranquil emperor, that your clemency grant me a kindly hearing, so that the purpose of my mind may be made clear to your gentleness. From a Christian emperor, the son of Constantine of holy memory, I ought to obtain this very thing without delay. Yet I understand that I am struggling here, because even with repeated apologies I cannot bring your mind, which is forgiving even toward the guilty, back into favor with me.

The speech your piety sent to the people some time ago wounds me greatly, though I must bear all things patiently. But it is a wonder to me that your mind, which is always given to gentleness and which, as it is written, never keeps its anger until the sun goes down, should still hold indignation against me. For I, most religious emperor, seek with you a true peace: not one composed of words with deceit hidden inside, but one reasonably confirmed by the precepts of the Gospels.

Not only the affair of Athanasius but many other matters came into the open, and on their account I had begged your gentleness that a council be held. Before all else, as the sincere devotion of your mind toward God especially desires, the cause of the faith, in which lies our first hope toward God, would be carefully dealt with. Then the affairs of those who ought to admire our reverence toward God could be settled. It would have been worthy of a worshipper of God, and worthy of your empire, which is ruled and increased by the goodness of Christ, for your clemency to grant us this very request, especially out of reverence for the holy religion to which you prudently attend.

But many are hastening to tear apart the members of the church. They have invented the story that I suppressed letters so that the crimes of the man whom they were said to have condemned would not become known to all, as if those letters of the bishops

of the Eastern and Egyptian bishops, all of which contained the same charges (against) Athanasius… But it is quite clear to everyone, and no one denies it, that we made known the letters of the Easterners, read them to the church, read them to the council, and also replied to the Easterners. We did not give our assent and judgment to these letters, because at that same time the judgment of eighty Egyptian bishops concerning Athanasius

contradicted them, and we likewise read that judgment aloud and communicated it to the Italian bishops. Hence it seemed contrary to the one law [?] to give our consent even in part, especially since the number of bishops supporting Athanasius was greater. Eusebius, who had been sent, left these writings with us when he hurried off to Africa, as he owes faith to God. Afterwards Vincent, who had been sent with the others, took all these writings to Arles, so that they would not be lacking when it came to obtaining a council.

Your prudence therefore sees that nothing entered my mind that it would have been unworthy for servants of God to think. God is my witness, and the whole church with all its members is witness, that by faith in my God and fear of him I trample, and have trampled, all worldly things underfoot, as the teaching of the Gospels and the apostles commands. I have done so not with rash fury but by divine law, established and observed. And while living as a churchman in another office, I fulfilled nothing that belonged to the law out of boastfulness, nothing out of desire for glory.

I came to this office unwillingly; my God is my witness. In it I desire to remain without offending God for as long as I am in this world. I have never brought it about that my own statutes should be confirmed and kept, but always the apostolic ones. Following the custom and order of my forebears, I have allowed nothing to be added to the episcopate of the city of Rome and nothing to be taken from it. And keeping the faith that has come down through the succession of so many bishops, several of whom were martyrs, I always desire that it be guarded unimpaired.

Finally, concern for the church and devotion itself now persuade me to lay the case open before your piety. The Easterners declare that they wish to be joined to us in peace. What peace is this, most clement emperor, when from those very regions there are four bishops, Demophilus, Macedonius, Eudoxius and Martyrius, who eight years ago at Milan refused to condemn the heretical opinion of Arius and walked out of the council in anger? Your fairness and clemency can judge what it would mean, and what danger it would hold, to give consent to the judgments of such men, if that is even right.

What they now attest so subtly, under pretext of Athanasius's name, is nothing new. There still exist letters that Bishop Alexander long ago sent to Silvester of holy memory. In them he reported that before the ordination of Athanasius he had expelled from the church eleven men, presbyters and deacons, because they followed the heresy of Arius. Some of these, now placed outside the catholic church, are said to have found conventicles for themselves, and George in Alexandria is said to be in communion with them by letter. What peace then can there be, most tranquil emperor, if bishops are hauled before tribunals, as has now happened throughout Italy, and forced to obey the judgments of such men?

Hear something else, since your tranquillity patiently allows it. There are letters, recently arrived, from the envoys who had been sent to your clemency. In them they report that because of the disturbance of all the churches they had indeed been willing at first to yield to the judgments of the Easterners. Yet they had set a condition: that if those same men

condemned the heresy of Arius, they themselves would give way on this basis and obey their judgments. The agreement, as they themselves report, was confirmed with a written document as witness. They go into the council, and after deliberation they receive the answer that the Easterners cannot condemn the doctrine of Arius, but that Athanasius (which was all they were demanding) must be deprived of communion. From this let your clemency consider also whether, while the right of the catholic religion is properly preserved, the case of a man ought to be carefully and thoroughly examined. Therefore again and again we ask your gentleness, and your mind devoted to God, by the power of him who has shown all mortals how great he is in your defense: keep before your eyes the benefits of him who rules your empire in all things, and have these matters carefully dealt with in an assembly of bishops with all due consideration. Then, the times having been made peaceful through you with God's favor and with your tranquillity's consent, let everything be examined so that what has stood confirmed by the judgment of the priests of God can be kept as an example for the future. That is, all [?] should agree to the exposition of faith that was confirmed among so many bishops at Nicaea in the presence of your father of holy memory. So the Savior himself, who looks down from above on the purpose of your mind, may rejoice that in settling such great affairs you have rightly placed the cause of faith and peace even before the needs of the state. To entreat your gentleness, therefore, to be pleased to hear our representations with a kindly mind, it was decided that my brother and fellow bishop, the holy man Lucifer, should set out with Pancratius the presbyter and Hilary the deacon. We believe that they can without difficulty obtain from your clemency a council for the peace of all the catholic churches. May the clemency of almighty God keep you safe for us, most clement (and most religious) Augustus. END.

SERIES B.
Preface. [?] I
I.

Filled with the Holy Spirit, the apostle Paul speaks thus to the Corinthians: And now faith, hope and love abide. In this way he embraces the great mystery of the truth that is to be fulfilled in a threefold disposition of the human mind. But the other things, whether offices or gifts, in which we are now engaged only in part, he indicates are to be done away when, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, the perfection of the heavenly counsel is reached. For when our corruption has been transformed into the glory of eternity, what

is now believed to be something will no longer be, when there begins to be granted that which, once it exists, is always eternal. But this is the merit of faith, hope and love: that when bodies are dissolved in paying the debt of death, they abide for ever and never cease, and although everything in a human being is only in part, these alone are perfect. For whether prophecies are done away, or tongues cease, or knowledge is destroyed, those three named first attain an unchangeable perfection; they will neither borrow anything from outside nor gain anything more abundant than what they already hold. For when absolute truth drives out prophecies and tongues and knowledge, eternity itself will take up faith, hope and love, the guides and patrons by which eternity is grasped, just as they will then be.

And the same blessed apostle distinguished the merits of each of these things according to the measure [?] of its honour, so that it might readily be understood that, while the rest are to be done away as heavenly growth advances, though not without the considerable fruit of their honour, these three alone are the ones that abide.

God, then, rewards with the prizes of righteousness the one who, though ignorant, believes that he is God. That is why faith first justifies Abraham; why the faith of the mother who put the Lord to the test amid his silence saves the daughter of the Canaanite woman; and why, in John, those who believe in his name are given power to be born of God. Great is the merit of faith, and perfect is the blessedness of those who believe God: through it, those born in the body, in iniquity and in sickness, receive righteousness and health and birth from God.

Hope, for its part, trusting in what God has ordained, rises above the pleasures of worldly life and the goods of a peaceful age, ready to earn future gains by the loss of present things. The Lord rewards it with this prize: Everyone who has left home or brothers or sisters or mother or children or field for my name's sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life. How splendid is the confidence of its expectation, a witness to the powers of God, despising all present things as nothing and uncertain, and grasping future things as eternal and already present!

But although the same apostle grants equal glory to faith, hope and love, which are to abide, and indicates that they are equally inviolable, he nevertheless shows that love surpasses the others named before it. For through love we are bound to God by a kind of chain of the love we have received, and once the love of devotion has been poured into his name, our will becomes inseparable from him; from it neither sword nor famine nor nakedness will separate us, and through it anger, rivalry, ambition, wickedness, luxury and greed are held in check. And therefore, while faith, hope and love abide, the greatest of these is love, through which those joined together in God's name by an undivided affection can be neither dissolved nor divided by any force of worldly upheaval.
To this great and weighty apostolic authority I too, among others, if I have any place after them, bear witness through

this love, laid up for us before the ages for those taken up into the hope of heaven. And I cleave to the name of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, rejecting the company of the wicked and the fellowship of the unbelieving. With them I was given the chance, like the others, to flourish in the good things of this world, to enjoy leisure at home, to abound in every advantage, to boast of the king's friendship, to be a bishop in name though falsely, and to become a heavy burden on each and all, publicly and privately, by lording it over the church — if only I would corrupt the truth of the gospel with falsehood, soothe a guilty conscience with the flattery of ignorance, defend a corrupt judgement by the excuse that the decision was someone else's, escape being held guilty of the sin of heresy, not through my own faith, which would certainly have been liable, but through the simple-mindedness of the ignorant, and feign integrity behind the difficulty the public has in understanding.

For love, abiding through faith and hope in Christ in simplicity of heart, would not tolerate this. And since I had received from the apostle: For we have not received a spirit of fear; and since we had learned from the Lord, who says: Everyone who confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven; and since the same Lord had said: Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven; blessed are you when they curse you and persecute you and say every evil against you for righteousness' sake; rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven — I could not prefer a self-seeking conscience in guilty silence to enduring injury for confessing God.

I am therefore attempting to bring to public knowledge a work that is weighty and many-sided: entangled by the devil's deceit, made subtle by the heretics' side, prejudged through the pretence and fear of many, foreign because of the distance between the places where it happened and where we now are, old in time, new because it has been kept silent, long passed over under a feigned peace, and recently revived by the impious cunning of the most deceitful men. It is a matter for which, even in the business of the Roman Empire, peace is disrupted [?], the king is anxious, the palace is in ferment, bishops rush about, officials of the Master of the Offices fly to and fro, and there is turmoil against apostolic men with every department in a hurry. Everywhere there is such activity, alarm and pressure that the very labour and care spent on securing this position has plainly betrayed its wickedness.

Indeed, I remember that it has long been said in common talk that certain priests of God are in exile because they will not pass sentence against Athanasius; and this error has taken hold of nearly everyone's mind, so that they think that, in his name, none of them had a sufficiently worthy cause for undergoing exile.

I pass over the point that, although the highest reverence must be paid to the king, since kingship comes from God, his judgement is nevertheless not to be calmly admitted into the decisions of bishops, because what is Caesar's is to be rendered to Caesar, and to God what is God's. I say nothing of the emperor's verdict given without any hearing of the case; I do not complain that a sentence is extorted against a man in his absence, although, as the apostle says, where faith is, there is freedom, and priestly simplicity ought not to tolerate this. But I pass these things over, not because they are to be despised, but because weightier matters lie beneath them.

I shall also give this advice, not without purpose: that careful attention be paid to this whole volume. For everything must be separated by date, distinguished by judgements, set apart by persons and weighed by the force of the words, so that no one, faced with so many letters and so many

synods brought forward again and again at that time, may be overcome by a harmful weariness before the end. (9). What we have always believed, we hold now as well; for experience proves and confirms what each has heard with his ears. True indeed is what the most blessed teacher of the Gentiles, the apostle Paul, said of himself: (Since you seek proof of him who speaks in me, Christ), although, since the Lord Christ dwelt in him, there can certainly be no doubt

that the Spirit spoke through his soul and sounded through the instrument of his body. So you too, dearest brother, though separated in body, were present with us in harmony of mind and will. And your reason for being absent was both honourable and necessary: that schismatic wolves might not steal and snatch by stealth, or heretical dogs, roused to rabid fury, bark madly, or indeed the serpent, the devil, pour out the venom of blasphemies. For this will seem best and most fitting: that the priests of the Lord should report from each and every province to the head, that is, to the see of the apostle Peter.

Since, then, everything that was done, transacted and decreed is contained in the documents, and the living voices of our dearest brothers and fellow presbyters Archidamus and Philoxenus and of our dearest son Leo the deacon will be able to set it out most truly and faithfully, it seems almost superfluous to repeat the same things in this letter. It became plain to all that those who came from the regions of the East, who call themselves bishops (though among them are certain ringleaders whose sacrilegious minds the Arian heresy has stained with its pestilential poison), after long evasion and out of distrust refused to come to judgment, and found fault with your communion and ours, which was without fault. For not only do we all alike believe in the innocence of Athanasius on the testimony of eighty bishops, but also, when they were summoned through your presbyters and by letter to the synod that was to be held in the city of Rome, they refused to come. And it would have been quite unjust, when they treated it with contempt and so many priests bore witness for Marcellus and Athanasius, to deny these two our fellowship.

There were three matters to be dealt with. For the most religious emperors themselves permitted everything to be examined and debated afresh, and above all the holy faith and the integrity of the truth, which these men have violated. The second concerned the persons who, they said, had been

deposed by an unjust judgment, so that, if they could prove it, a just confirmation might be made. The third question, which truly deserves to be called a question, was that they had inflicted grave and bitter injuries, and even intolerable and wicked outrages, on the churches: they seized bishops, presbyters, deacons and all the clergy, sent them into exile, carried them off to desert places, and killed them with hunger, thirst, nakedness and every kind of want. Others they shut up in prison and wore them down with squalor and stench; some they put in iron chains, so that their necks were throttled by very tight collars. In fact, some of them

died in chains under that same unjust punishment, and there can be no doubt that their death was made glorious by martyrdom. Even now they dare to keep some in custody, and there was no ground for any charge except that they resisted and cried out that they abhorred the Arian and Eusebian heresy and would not have communion with such men; whereas those who preferred to serve the world have profited [?]. And those who had previously been deposed were not only received back but even promoted to clerical rank, and received the reward of their falsehood.

Hear, most blessed brother, what was decreed concerning the impious and ignorant young men Ursacius and Valens. It was plain that they did not cease to scatter the deadly seeds of adulterated doctrine, and that Valens had left his own church and sought to invade another. At the time when he stirred up sedition, one of our brothers, Viator, who was unable to flee, was knocked down and trampled in that same city of Aquileia, and died on the third day. The cause of his death was certainly Valens, who stirred up the disorder and incited it.

But when you read what we have reported to the most blessed Augusti, you will readily see that we have left nothing out, so far as reason allowed. And so that a long narrative might not be tiresome, we have briefly indicated what they did and what crimes they committed.
Your outstanding prudence must see to it that through your letters our brothers in Sicily, in Sardinia and in Italy learn what was done and what was decided, so that they may not

(16). The matter, I think, needs no further discourse to explain it. Everything has been set out and stated so plainly that it has been brought into the full light of knowledge: the witnesses from Egypt were suborned, Athanasius himself was present, the false judges fled shamefully by night, driven by their conscience,

and the heavy odium of such great crimes was laid before the eyes of all. Add to this the origin of the case, from which a pretext for a sentence against Athanasius was sought. He is accused on the ground that an altar was overturned by an assault of his presbyter at the very time of the sacrifice, while the presbyter Ischyras was officiating. It is denied that Ischyras is a presbyter, and the false charge is condemned together with its author. Moreover, the work of the sacrifice could not have been carried out without a presbyter. And while the man is thus in question, there is no place at all for so grave a deed: in the Mareotis there is no church. Did the sanctity of the ground itself give way, or did the site of the violated sacrifice sink into some chasm, as sometimes happens? Ischyras is claimed to have been ordained bishop straight from deacon, so that the lying bishop might carry greater authority about the outrage he suffered as a presbyter. But if the church building existed, it still exists; if it does not exist, it never did.

And what doubt can there be that it was rather these judges of false charges who asserted that something had been done which plainly was never done, and not those who judged afterwards and established that something had not existed which, had it existed, could not fail to exist still?

If, then, anyone has been trained in human institutions for the use of common understanding, if anyone follows the precepts of prudence along the path of pursuing the truth, let him pay attention and weigh what judgment he would wish to hold in affairs of this kind.

I say nothing for the moment about the authors of the judgments. Suppose there are these two verdicts: one that affirms the crime, names the place of the crime, and identifies the man who suffered the injury; the other that denies the crime, the place and the man. I ask which verdict it will seem fair for you to accept. Surely, I think, anyone consulted by both sides and placed between the two verdicts will speak thus: 'If there is a crime, it must be proved; if there is a place, it must be shown; if there is a man, he must be produced.' But when there is no evidence of the deed, no sacred place, and no injured man, it will be thought madness for a judge to pass judgment on things that do not exist.

Look up to heaven and the stars, you priests, and fix your gaze on him who made them out of nothing, with the freedom of the faith and hope you have received, remembering that this pattern of the judgment to come upon you has been set before you: With the judgment you pronounce you will be judged. Answer me when I ask: 'By what judgment did you condemn Athanasius?'

You will say, of course, 'By the judgment of bishops,' and that will be the excuse for your confession. 'We followed,' you say, 'the holy reverence due to judgments made within episcopal communion.' But will you deny that you knew communion had been restored to Athanasius by Hosius, Maximinus and Julius—the Athanasius whose condemnation Valens, Ursacius and Saturninus demanded of you? I am not making communion the issue; I am asking what your verdict was on the charge against Athanasius.

His presbyter Macarius is said to have burst into a church in the Mareotis, thrown the presbyter Ischyras into confusion, and cast down the sacraments of our salvation. A catechumen and a pagan were questioned as witnesses to this. But do you not know that it was afterwards judged by holy men that there was no church in the Mareotis and that Ischyras was not a presbyter? What, then, was it that you followed?

You give authority to false bishops and deny it to true ones; you decree that what exists does not exist, and you pass judgment on what does not exist. But to make you believe this trumped-up charge, I suppose, a prison compelled you, a guard pressed upon you, a torturer bore down on you, a sword hung over you, fire burned you! In judging things that do not exist, wickedness has won episcopal authority among you; in upholding the truth, holiness has lost credit. O true disciples of Christ! O worthy successors of Peter and Paul! O devout fathers of the church! O ambitious envoys between God

and the people—you have sold the truth of Christ for the falsehood of men! We have therefore fulfilled our first proposition, in which we undertook to show that Athanasius could not be held guilty of any of the crimes charged against him. It remains for me to say in very few words what was done about Marcellus and Photinus.

Photinus, bishop of Sirmium, had been schooled by Marcellus; for he had also served for some time as a deacon under him. Having corrupted the ways and disciplines of innocence, he persisted in disturbing the truth of the Gospel with new teachings. And it often happens that, when the growth

of vices has caused losses in the love of God, a mad zeal for depraved knowledge increases. So, to remove from the episcopate Photinus, who two years earlier had already been condemned as a heretic at the synod of Milan, priests gathered from a great many provinces, all the more anxious and troubled that everything was again being thrown into confusion, because some time before it had become necessary to cut off from the church a number of bishops who were guilty either of the false judgments against Athanasius

or of communion with the Arian heresy. Seizing this opportunity, Ursacius and Valens approached the bishop of the people of Rome, begged to be received into the church, and asked to be admitted to communion through pardon. Julius, after taking counsel, granted the pardon they begged, so that, to the gain of the catholic church, he might also weaken the Arians, by admitting into catholic communion, through the pardon of restored peace, men who had earlier disturbed unity but now repented of their design and audacity. (20) And because confession can only be of the truth, repentance only of a fault, and pardon only of a wrong committed, Valens and Ursacius, in order to be admitted to communion as they asked, first made profession in letters such as these concerning the innocence of Athanasius, the falsity of the judgment, and the guilt of the Arian heresy.
