So, once the letters above had been given, pardon was granted to those who asked for it, and a return to the catholic faith together with communion was bestowed on them, especially since the very letters of those begging pardon upheld the truth of the synod of Serdica. (21) Meanwhile, however, a council met at Sirmium. Photinus, exposed as a heretic, long since pronounced guilty and long since cut off from the communion of unity, could not even then be removed, because of the partisanship of the people.

***** But this same Athanasius separated from his communion Marcellus—who, after the reading of the book he had written and published (for we too have it), had been restored to his episcopate by the sentence of the synod of Serdica—when he perceived that Marcellus was mixing in certain other novelties and, by ambiguous preaching, seeking a path toward the doctrine into which Photinus broke out. He did so before Photinus was charged, showing that he had anticipated by his judgment the design of a corrupt will, and not condemning him on account of the publication of the book. But since it is easy for evil to be made out of good, this lent authority not to what had previously been done against Marcellus, but to what was to be done against Photinus.

Everyone ought to know, however, that no synod was ever afterwards convened against Marcellus except the one whose sentence was annulled by the decisions of Serdica, and that not even when the Westerners made a decree concerning Photinus and reported it to the Easterners was any judgment pronounced against him. Rather, men cunning in mind, subtle in wit and persistent in malice sought an occasion to reopen the judgment that had been annulled by the acquittal of Athanasius, and in writing back about Photinus they added a mention of Marcellus as though he were the teacher of such doctrines. Their aim was that the novelty of the case might rouse once more into public memory the question about Athanasius himself, which had already died with time and been buried by the judgment of truth, and that the name of Marcellus, creeping in through the condemnation of Photinus, might bring it back.

Now it stands in the body of the earlier letter that Marcellus was condemned by the Arians together with Athanasius on account of the book he had published on the subjection of the Lord Christ. It is also shown that he was found innocent when that same book was read. The book itself, which is still extant, likewise proves the falsity of the Arian judgment. Concerning Photinus, however, letters were sent to the Easterners only as custom required—not to extort their assent by wrong, as is now being done, but by the usual practice of informing everyone.

But why, when communion had been refused to Marcellus, is Athanasius declared guilty in their reply? Was Marcellus excluded because of some fault in his book? They themselves bear witness that Photinus took the beginnings of this perversity from his teachings. For when Athanasius refused him communion, Marcellus kept himself from entering the church. Thus the communion once entered into with him attests his faith regarding the subjection and handing over of the kingdom, while its refusal in turn shows the depravity of the other doctrine.

And so both of this man's judgments are free from blame: in granting communion he followed the assent of the synod, while in refusing it he acted alone, without any synodal authority, Marcellus himself having withdrawn. But this whole question belongs to another cause and another grievance. And although they are satisfying their long-conceived hatred of Athanasius, so great a scheme nevertheless proceeds to a still greater degree of crime.
For my third point allows me to show that the faith which they set out at the beginning of their letter is fraudulent and heretical, and steeped in hidden poison beneath flattering words.

For they profess thus: that there is indeed one unbegotten God the Father and one only Son of his, God from God, light from light, the firstborn of all creation, and they add a third, the Holy Spirit the Paraclete—so that, once the vigilance of readers or the simplicity of the unlearned had been caught by such soft opening words, by one and the same assent of an extorted signature

they might be carried over to the punishment of Photinus, the condemnation of Athanasius, and the condemnation of the catholic faith. And I hope that the synod of Serdica has contributed no small part to the understanding of this matter, for there it is shown that all the charges against Athanasius were fabricated through the persecution of the Arians, and that force was applied to the people of God to make them pass over into a pestilent complicity with a deadly doctrine. Yet since the case requires it, I will set out the whole matter briefly.

It was always the care and business of apostolic men, by constant and public preaching of the perfect faith, to suppress every attempt of barking heresy and, by setting forth the truth of the Gospels, to extinguish the perversity of erring doctrine, lest it stain the minds of its hearers with some blemish and infect them with the contagion of a clinging vice.

Therefore in various letters they set out diligently, frequently and fully what belief there ought to be concerning God the Father, what knowledge concerning the Son of God, and what sanctification in the Holy Spirit, so that the Son might be known as God from God the Father, and God the Father in God the Son, and God the Son in God the Father. And so, according to the definition of him who said, I and the Father are one, and again, As you, Father, are in me and

I in you, our faith is contained: in the names and persons of Father and Son, one God. For neither the envy of the Jews, nor the hatred of the Gentiles, nor the fury of the heretics has been stirred up against us for any other reason than that we confess the eternity, the power and the name of the Son in the Father. The perversity of heretics, on the other hand, has always sprung from an impious faith. For while, taken up with vices and turned away from the works of innocence, they entangle themselves in the difficulties of useless questions, having become reprobate in life, will and judgment, they seek to win favor by novelty of doctrine, now that they have lost the knowledge of the truth.

When, therefore, it had become known to our fathers that the two Ariuses had appeared as preachers of a most profane faith, and that this taint had spread further, no longer as a mere opinion but as a settled conviction, they hastened together from every part of the world and assembled at Nicaea, so that, once the faith had been set forth to the peoples and the way of divine knowledge made straight in the light of understanding, the seeds of the emerging evil might be killed within their very authors. Now the Ariuses taught such things as this:

'that God the Father begot the Son for the purpose of establishing the world, and by his own power made from nothing, into a new and different substance, a new and different God.' They were profane toward the Father, supposing that something like him could be begotten from nothing; blasphemous toward Christ, stripping him of the nobility of the Father's infinity. Thus, though they had learned from the person of the Father, There is no other God besides me, and from the Son, I am in the Father and the Father in me, and, I and the Father are one, they broke the bond of holy unity in both, assigning to the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, the substance of a creature that once did not exist [?], a beginning in time, an origin from nothing, and a name from another.

So, to suppress this evil, three hundred or more bishops were assembled at Nicaea. By the assent of all, all the Arians were condemned as heretics, and, once the teachings of the Gospels and the apostles had been unfolded, the perfect light of catholic unity was brought forth. What was expressed there, the faith itself, as it was set forth, makes plain.
HERE BEGINS THE FAITH WRITTEN AT NICAEA BY 318 BISHOPS AGAINST ALL HERESIES.
We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of things visible and invisible.

And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born of the Father, that is, of the substance of the Father, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, born, not made, of one substance with the Father (what the Greeks call homoousion), through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who for us men and for our salvation came down and became

incarnate, became man, suffered, and rose again on the third day, ascended into the heavens, and will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit. But those who say, 'There was when he was not,' and 'Before he was born he was not,' and that 'he was made from things that did not exist' (what the Greeks call ex ouk onton), or who say that the Son of God is of another substance, or 'mutable and changeable'—these the catholic and apostolic church anathematizes.
Narrative text.

(28). Comparing one creed with the other exposes the falseness of their intention. The creed drawn up at Nicaea is full and complete. Every approach by which heretics usually creep in is barred on every side, and it is held together by the inviolable solidity of the eternal unity between the Father and the Son. This creed, however, flatters with simplicity, first asserting that we believe in this way, which God forbid anyone should.

The faith of the Westerners, by contrast, is founded on the teachings of the gospel. It confesses the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father; the Father unbegotten, and the Son eternal by the substance of eternity. That is, just as the Father always is, so the Son too is always in the Father, and is God born of God, not conceived, being always in him from whom he is.

But this is treachery, not faith. By saying “God from God,” commending the word “firstborn” and establishing the name of the Trinity, it hides its poison under a modest show of religious restraint. It says “God from God” and “light from light” so that, under cover of this confession, he may be taken to have come into being as God and light made by God out of God and light, not begotten of God, that is, not from the substance of the Father's eternity. In this way the Father is insulted and the Son too is cheapened, if he is a God who arose from nothing. In confessing him “firstborn,” they assign a certain order, starting from his origin, to the creation of the things of the world. Since the world is from time, Christ, though prior to the world, is also from time. On this view there is in him no eternity before the ages, only an order in time among created things. Something is therefore left that existed before him, since he began to be at a point in time. And everything that is God is dissolved in Christ, since his origin, from Mary, who once did not exist, is from time.

Moreover, these men, empty of all good hope, stretch the apostle's authority to exploit so great a danger, because it was said of him, “firstborn of all creation.” They strip away the statements before and after it and, using the apostle's name, build up support for their own doctrines. For the words run in this order: Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, because in him all things were established in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all.

So “the image of the invisible God” comes from nothing, I suppose, and began in time! Or, because he is “the firstborn of all creation,” he is meant to express some order of a creation joined to him and born along with him! But do not these words follow “firstborn of all creation”: “because in him all things were established in heaven and on earth”? That is, in him the matter of all the elements, visible and invisible, was founded and established, and for that reason “all things are through him and in him.” He is therefore “the firstborn of all creation” because from the very beginning all the beginnings of the generations of everything he was going to make were already established in him. So he is not first in number in the order of creatures, which were established in order. Rather he himself, “the image of the invisible God,” abiding always in himself through the power of making, held the place of firstborn over the things, visible and invisible, that would be created through him in heaven and on earth and come into existence.

Their falsehood is woven together in much the same way when they name the Trinity. With impious and slanderous mouth they separate the Son from the Father by different substances, so that authority rests in two separate beings, and then a third is counted in the Spirit. Yet the Father is in the Son, the Son is in the Father, and the Holy Spirit receives from both. The Spirit is the very one in whom the inviolable unity of this holy Trinity is expressed, and yet the Trinity as they proclaim it gives birth to division on the heretics' side.

But the careful document of Nicaea, with its perfect wording, shut in all the devices of the heretics with a very strict rule of truth. It states: We believe in one God the Father and in his one Son Jesus Christ. Both are “one,” and each is “one”: “one” is said both of the personal name of the Father and of the Son, because “one” is said of each. “True God from true God” teaches that both the power and the name are common to both with equal truth. Nothing is to be supposed in one that is different from the other, since, as God from God and true from true, both are one.

Since there is one in both, “born, not made” refers to the distinctive character of his birth and origin. Being made comes from nothing, whereas being born of the Father is proper to him, and those who are born have no other form or power than that of their origin. What is made comes into being through a work, in order to be made. So in him there is no making that began from nothing, but a birth from a parent.

Now “of one substance with the Father,” which the Greeks call homoousion, means this. Eternity alone is like itself, and what always is, is in God. So the truth of essence is set forth in the Lord Jesus Christ to keep any stain of heretical depravity from falling on him. Essence is named from what always is. Because it has never needed outside help to sustain itself, it is also called “substance,” since it subsists within itself as what always is, in the power of its own eternity. And so he says: I and the Father are one; and: He who has seen me has seen the Father too; and again: I am in the Father and the Father in me; and: I came forth from the Father. He is equal in both, that is,

one and the same substance of eternity is fulfilled in both, in God who is unbegotten and in God who is begotten. As for the words “he came down,” “was incarnate,” “was made man” and “rose on the third

day,” “ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead,” these contain the mysteries of our salvation. The Son of God is called “unchangeable” and “unalterable” because in taking on manhood he brought glory to corruption, rather than a stain to eternity. And the anathema against those who say he was “made from nothing,” which the Greeks call ex ouk onton, and who say “There was when he was not” and “Before he was born he was not,” places under a curse those who would violate the eternity in Christ, that is, the Father's deity.

Athanasius, a deacon at the synod of Nicaea and afterwards bishop of Alexandria, had been a vigorous champion of making this faith known to all. Holding fast to the truth, he had overcome the Arian plague throughout Egypt,

and for that reason false charges were contrived against him through conspiring witnesses. The matter was later settled by the verdicts of faithful judges. But it will greatly help understanding to learn what address the synod of Serdica sent to the emperor Constantius after Athanasius was acquitted. END.

HERE BEGINS A COPY OF THE LETTER OF LIBERIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME, TO THE EASTERN BISHOPS.
To our most beloved brothers and fellow bishops, all those appointed throughout the East, Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, sends eternal greeting.

Following the tradition of our forebears, I then sent presbyters of the city of Rome, Lucius, Paul and Aelianus, from my own side to the aforesaid Athanasius in Alexandria, asking him to come to the city of Rome, so that whatever church discipline required might be decided about him in person.

Through the same presbyters I also sent him a letter stating that if he did not come, he should know that he was cut off from the communion of the Roman church. The presbyters returned and reported that he had refused to come.

I have therefore followed the letter your charity sent us about the aforesaid Athanasius. Know by this letter, which I have sent to your unanimity, that I am at peace with all of you and with all the bishops of the catholic church, but that the aforesaid Athanasius is cut off from my communion, that is, from that of the Roman church, and from the fellowship of church letters.
Narrative text

What is there in this letter that does not show holiness, that does not come from the fear of God? But Potamius and Epictetus, as is recorded in the synod of Ariminum, were so glad to condemn the bishop of the city of Rome that they refused to listen to this.

Moreover, Bishop Fortunatianus achieved nothing by sending this same letter again to various bishops. By denying communion to Athanasius, Liberius would rather become a burden to himself and bring the whole danger of the affair upon himself, so long as he took nothing away from the synod of Serdica, at which Athanasius had been acquitted and the Arians condemned. Letters sent from all of Egypt and from Alexandria made this point. Such letters had once been written to Julius about restoring communion to the exiled Athanasius, and now, as will be understood from what is attached below, similar ones were sent to Liberius about upholding it. END.
IV.
LIKEWISE A COPY OF THE LETTER OF LIBERIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME,
WRITTEN TO THE CATHOLIC BISHOPS OF ITALY.
Liberius to the catholic bishops living throughout Italy, eternal greeting in the Lord.

Whoever comes to his senses blots out the fault of ignorance. This can also be seen in the holy Scriptures. We read that godliness is useful for all things, and that bodily exercise gives way to it, though bodily exercise too keeps some fruit of usefulness.

The circumstances of the present time also require us to pursue this godliness. Perhaps someone among those who pursue this study [?] has considered the matter and decided, with too harsh a censure, to shamelessly destroy and alter what apostolic authority has already secured concerning godliness. He holds that no pardon should be given to those who acted in ignorance at Ariminum, for whom it was not permitted not to know [?] that once caught they would fall into death. Even so, severity is not to be rejected for that reason.

But it falls to me to weigh everything with moderation, especially since all the Egyptians and the Achaeans have adopted this view and received many back. Those we have discussed above should indeed be pardoned. But the authors should be condemned, who with a crooked and malicious subtlety of darkness offended the minds of the innocent, and so drew a veil over the truth, claiming that darkness is light and light is darkness.

Someone may have been caught by ignorance and experienced in himself that pestilential poison of the Arian doctrine, crafty and hidden. If he now comes to his senses at the very gentle summons of our word, let him be restored and drain it out. Let him condemn it and rage all the more vehemently against its authors, whom he has found violent toward himself. Let him commit himself wholly and afresh to the apostolic and catholic faith as set down at the assembly of the synod of Nicaea. By this profession, even though to some it seems a light and lenient thing, let him recover what he had lost through cunning against what is right [?].

But someone may be found with a mind so stupid, which I hardly believe, that he not only refuses to be converted by taking the antidote of health, but even thinks he should claim the harmful poison and venom for himself. He will be overcome by reason, handed over in his ruin to the author of the treachery, and punished by the spiritual vigour of the catholic church. END.

To our most beloved brothers throughout Illyricum who hold the faith of the fathers, the bishops of Italy send eternal greeting in the Lord.

(3). It is by the grace of a divine gift that, as the apostle says, we have all begun to think the same thing and all to confess the same thing. As far as Italy is concerned, it recognized the fraud it suffered at Ariminum and long ago returned to the faith of the fathers, that is, the faith written at Nicaea. we congratulate you that it has cast off the fellowship of unbelief that weighed it down and has begun to approve what belongs to right doctrine. Receive, then, most beloved brothers, our one and the same judgment, made firm by our signatures. V. HERE BEGINS A COPY OF THE LETTER OF VALENS, URSACIUS AND OTHERS TO GERMINIUS.
To our most religious lord and brother Germinius, Valens, Ursacius, Gaius and Paul.
When concern for hope and salvation weighs on us, those who show concern deserve praise rather than reproach. And salvation and hope rest above all in the catholic faith.

Our lords, brothers and fellow bishops Valens and Paul admonished you at a meeting, and you were unwilling to answer the rumour that is spread about you, most religious lord. Yet you testified in your letter that you persevere in the same charity and are ready to show unimpaired love toward us. Therefore we, gathered together at Singidunum, remind your holiness once more by this letter to set aside every pretext for evasion and kindly write back to us again. We ask you to state more openly that you will not depart, as you have already professed, from the catholic faith that was set out and confirmed at Ariminum by the holy council, to which all the bishops of the East also agreed.

That faith is this, as laid down in it: “We say that the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures,” not “according to substance” or “in all things,” but simply. For if this statement is altered, the treacherous assertion of the late Basil will plainly be revived, the assertion on account of which the synod was held and which was deservedly condemned.

Kindly declare plainly in your letter, then, what we ask: that you have not said, and do not and will not say, “that the Son is like the Father in all things except unbegottenness.” Otherwise the claim of the bearers of your letter, Jovian the deacon and Martyrius the subdeacon, will seem more credible. In their plea before my aforesaid lords, our brothers and fellow bishops Valens and Paul, they asserted that you profess “that the Son is like the Father in all things.”

If your writings make it clear that you think as we have wished, then the complaint about the injury that certain of your clergy did to our brothers and fellow bishops Palladius and Gaius will not touch your reputation, even though you were unwilling to investigate it as you were admonished at the first meeting. The clergy themselves, of course, will answer for their own rashness.

We have sent this to your charity through Secundianus the presbyter, Pullentius the reader and Candidianus the exorcist, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of the most noble Gratian and Dagalaifus, keeping a copy for ourselves.
VI. HERE BEGINS THE REPLY OF GERMINIUS TO RUFIANUS, PALLADIUS AND THE OTHERS.
To my lords and most religious brothers Rufianus, Palladius, Severinus, Nichas, Heliodorus, Romulus, Mucianus and Stercorius, Germinius sends greeting in the Lord.

We have learned from the report of Vitalis, a man of senatorial rank serving in the office of the exalted prefecture, that your holiness wishes to be told plainly what it is in our faith that displeases Valens, Ursacius, Gaius and Paul. I thought it necessary to make this known to your holiness in this letter, and to state what I trust has also been in your own hearts from the beginning.

We hold what we received as handed down from the fathers and from the divine Scriptures, what we learned once for all and teach every day. Christ, the Son of God, our Lord, is like the Father in all things except unbegottenness. He is God from God, light from light, power from power, whole from whole, perfect from perfect, begotten before the ages and before everything that can be understood or spoken. No one knows his birth except the Father alone, as the Son himself asserts: For no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.

Through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made, according to the divine words of the Son himself, our Saviour, who says: My Father is working until now, and I am working; and again: For whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does too; and again: I and the Father are one; and again: He who has seen me has seen the Father too; and again: As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself; and again: As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he will; and again: Believe in God, and believe in me; and again: For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father.

And again, to whom did the Father say: Let us make man in our image and likeness? He did not say “in your image” or “in my image,” so as not to suggest any unlikeness in the divinity of his Son. Instead he joined them together, “in our image and likeness,” to show that his Son is God, like himself in all things. Again the evangelist says: We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth. And the apostle writes to the Corinthians: In whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that they do not shine with the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. And again the same apostle: And he has transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of

sins, who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. And again the same apostle: Have this mind among you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. Who would not understand that, just as our flesh was truly in Christ in the form of a servant, so too in the form of God the Father's divinity is truly in the Son? And again: See that no one leads you astray through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ;

for in him the whole fullness of the divinity dwells bodily. If, then, the whole fullness of the divinity dwells in Christ, he is not partly like and partly unlike, as those men now claim who, contending for their own desires, have gone backward and turned themselves away from us.

They think they are bringing forth something great from the divine Scriptures when they say that Christ is a “thing made” and a “creature.” We, on the contrary, following the Scriptures, also call him “way” and “door,” “stone of stumbling” and “rock of offence,” “foundation,” “arm” and “hand,” “wisdom” and “word,” “lamb” and “sheep,” “shepherd” and “priest,” “vine” and “vine,” and other things.

But we understand and speak of all these in such a way as to understand the powers and works of the Son of God. We do not liken his divine birth from the Father to names of this kind, for all things were made from nothing through the Son, but the Son is not from nothing; he was begotten from God the Father.

I am surprised that the aforesaid Valens has either forgotten, or is surely craftily concealing, what was done and defined in the past. Under the emperor Constantius of good memory, when dissension about the faith had begun among certain people, a meeting was held in the presence of that same emperor. Present were George, bishop of the church of the Alexandrians, Pancratius, bishop of the Pelusians, Basil, then bishop of Ancyra, and also Valens himself, Ursacius and my humble self. After a dispute about the faith that lasted into the night and was brought to a definite rule, Mark, chosen by all of us, dictated the creed. In that creed it is written: “the Son like the Father in all things, as the holy Scriptures say and teach.” We all agreed to this complete profession and signed it with our own hands.

If the spirit of this world now suggests something else to them, we cannot yet know it openly. We have professed from the Scriptures that the Son is like the Father in all things except unbegottenness. Let them in turn set out from the Scriptures how he is like in part and unlike in part.

And so, most beloved brothers, I have sent this profession fearlessly and without delay for your love to know. I have sent it through Cyriacus, an official, the first opportunity I found after the deacon Carinius, whom I sent to you. My purpose is that through your most watchful

devotion toward God it may also be made known to the whole brotherhood, so that no one may be entangled unawares in the snares of the deceitful devil. It is now for your unanimity to write back to me what the Holy Spirit suggests to you. I must inform your charity that I could not sign this letter because my hand was hurting, but I have instructed our brothers and fellow presbyters Innocent, Octavius and Catulus to sign it. END.
VII. Letters of Liberius and narrative text.
[?] VI. Narrative text.
Before he went into exile, Liberius wrote this letter, in identical form, to the confessors who were then in exile, that is, to Eusebius, Dionysius and Lucifer.
Letter to Eusebius, Dionysius and Lucifer (355).

The enemy of the human race may seem to have raged more violently against the members of the Church under the guise of peace. Yet your outstanding and singular faith has shown that you are priests most acceptable to God and approved by God even here, and has already marked you out as martyrs for the glory to come. Placed as I am between grief at your absence and joy at your glory, I simply cannot find the words of praise or the cry of exultation with which to proclaim the merits of your virtue. I only know that I offer you a more fitting consolation here if you believe that I have been thrust into exile together with you.

Indeed, I am deeply saddened that I am still left hanging in expectation, and that a harsher necessity keeps me from your fellowship for the time being. For I had wished, most devoted brothers, to be spent first on behalf of all of you, so that your love might instead follow an example of glory set by me. But let this be the palm of your merits: that you came first, through perseverance in the faith, to the illustrious glory of confession.

I beg you, therefore, beloved, to believe that I am present with you, to feel that in affection I am not absent, and to understand how greatly I grieve at being separated from your fellowship for the time being. How great a glory you have attained, you can better know from this: those who were crowned in persecution could feel only the bloody swords of the persecutor, but you, soldiers of God devoted in all things, have experienced even false brothers as enemies and have carried off the victory over the faithless. The more their violence was able to grow in the world, the more they are found to confer rewards of praise on the priests. So be secure in the heavenly promise.

And since you have been brought nearer to God, lift me up to the Lord by your prayers, me your fellow priest and a servant of God, so that I may bear with patience the assaults that come upon me, which day by day, as they are reported, inflict heavier wounds; so that, with my faith

inviolate and the standing of the Catholic Church preserved, the Lord may deign to make me equal to you. And since I wish to know more accurately what was done at the assembly itself, I beseech your holiness to deign to report everything faithfully by letter, so that both my mind, which is tormented by various rumors, and the strength of my body, which is already worn down, may feel a fresh increase from your encouragement. And in another hand: May God keep you safe, my lord brothers.
Narrative text.

From the letter to Ossius (368/4).

Meanwhile, since I ought to keep nothing from your knowledge, many fellow bishops from Italy came together who had joined me in petitioning the most religious emperor Constantius to order a council to be assembled at Aquileia, as he himself had earlier been pleased to do. I inform your holiness that Vincent of Capua, together with Marcellus, likewise a bishop from Campania, undertook our embassy. I had high hopes of him, since he understood the case very well and had often sat as judge in that same case with your holiness, and so I had believed that the law of the Gospels, or of the embassy, could be kept intact. Not only did he obtain nothing, but he himself was also drawn into that pretence. After what he did I was stricken with a double grief, and resolved that I must rather die for God, lest I should appear as the latest of the informers, or lend my consent to sentences against the Gospel.
Narrative text.

(4) After all these things that Liberius had either done or promised, once he had been sent into exile he brought them all to nothing by writing to the Arian heretics, those transgressors who had passed an unjust sentence against holy Athanasius, the orthodox bishop.
Letter to the Eastern bishops (357).
Liberius to his most beloved brothers, the presbyters and fellow bishops of the East, greeting.

(5) Because of your godly fear, your holy faith is known to God and to men of good will. As the law says, "Judge justly, you sons of men." I did not defend Athanasius; but because Julius of good memory, my predecessor, had received him, I was afraid that I might perhaps be judged a transgressor in some respect.

But when it pleased God and I learned that you had condemned him justly, I at once gave my consent to your sentences. I likewise gave a letter concerning him, that is, concerning his condemnation, to our brother Fortunatianus to be carried to the emperor Constantius. Therefore, now that Athanasius has been removed from the communion of all of us, and I am not to receive even his letters, I declare that I have peace with all of you and with all the Eastern bishops, and peace and unanimity throughout all the provinces.

For you may know more surely that in this letter of mine I am setting forth the true faith: my lord and our common brother Demophilus has kindly deigned to set out to me your faith, the catholic one, which was discussed, set out and received at Sirmium by many of our brothers and fellow bishops [This is the Arian perfidy; I have noted this, not the apostate Liberius. What follows is Liberius's:] by all who were present. This I accepted with a willing mind [Holy Hilary pronounces an anathema on him: Anathema on you from me, Liberius, and on your associates], I contradicted it in nothing, I gave my consent; this I follow, this I hold. [Anathema on you again, and a third time, Liberius the transgressor.]

I have indeed thought it right to ask your holiness, since you now see that I agree with you in everything, to deign by common counsel and effort to work for my release from exile and my return to the see that was divinely entrusted to me.
Narrative text.

(7) As for the [?] drawn up at Sirmium, which Liberius calls catholic and says was set out to him by Demophilus, these are the men who composed it: Narcissus, Theodore, Basil, Eudoxius, Demophilus, Cecropius, Silvanus, Ursacius, Valens, Evagrius, Irenaeus, Exuperantius, Terentianus, Bassus, Gaudentius, Macedonius, Mark, Acacius, Julius, Surinus, Simplicius and Junior [to be noted: all heretics].
LIKEWISE LIBERIUS, FROM EXILE, TO URSACIUS, VALENS AND GERMINIUS

(8) I know that you are sons of peace and that you also love the concord and unanimity of the Catholic Church. For this reason, not driven by any necessity (I say it with God as my witness) but for the good of peace and concord,

which is preferred even to martyrdom, I address you by this letter, my dearest lord brothers. Let your prudence know, then, that Athanasius, who was bishop of the church of Alexandria, (was condemned by me) before I wrote to the court of the holy emperor in accordance with the letter of the Eastern bishops, (and that) he was separated from the communion of the Roman church, as the whole presbyterate of the Roman church can testify. There was only one reason

why I seemed rather slow to send a letter about him to our brothers and fellow bishops of the East: that my legates, whom I had sent from the city of Rome to the court, and the bishops who had been deported, might, if possible, be recalled from exile along with them.

I also want you to know that I asked brother Fortunatianus to carry to the most clement emperor the letter I had written to the Eastern bishops, so that they too might know that I, together with them, am separated from the communion of Athanasius. I trust that His Piety will receive it gladly for the good of peace. I have also sent a copy of it to Hilary, the emperor's faithful eunuch. Let your charity see that I have done this with a kind and innocent mind.

Therefore by this letter of mine I address you and adjure you by God almighty and by Christ Jesus his Son, our God and Lord, to deign to go to the most clement emperor Constantius Augustus and ask him, for the good of peace and concord, in which His Piety always rejoices, to order me to return to the church divinely entrusted to me,

so that in his times the Roman church may suffer no tribulation. You should know from this letter of mine, dearest brothers, that I have peace with all of you, bishops of the Catholic Church, in a fair and simple spirit. For you will win great consolation for us on the day

of retribution if through you peace is restored to the Roman church. I also want our brothers and fellow bishops Epictetus and Auxentius to learn through you that I have peace and ecclesiastical communion with them. I believe they will receive this gladly. But whoever dissents from our peace and concord, which by God's will has been established throughout the world, let him know that he is separated from our communion. [Anathema pronounced by me on the transgressor, together with the Arians.]
LIKEWISE LIBERIUS, FROM EXILE, TO VINCENT.

(10) I do not teach your holy mind, dearest brother, but I remind it that evil conversations corrupt good morals. You know well the snares of evil men, through which I have come to this hardship; pray that the Lord may grant me endurance.
My most beloved son Urbicus the deacon, whom I seemed to have as a comfort, has been taken away from me by Venerius, an imperial agent.

But I have thought it right to inform your holiness that I have withdrawn from that contention over Athanasius and have sent a letter concerning him to our brothers and fellow bishops of the East. Therefore, since by God's will we have peace everywhere, you will deign to call together all the bishops of Campania and make these things known to them. Together with a number of them, write a letter of your own to the most clement emperor about our unanimity and peace, so that I too may be freed from my sorrow.

And in his own hand: May God keep you safe, brother. Likewise a page written out in his own hand: We have peace with all the Eastern bishops, and with you. I have discharged my duty before God. It is for you to see to it, if you want me to waste away in exile; God will be judge between me and you.
VIII.
COPY OF THE LETTER OF THE EASTERN BISHOPS, WHICH THEY GAVE TO THE ENVOYS ON THEIR RETURN FROM ARIMINUM.

Silvanus, Sophronius, Neon, Herodianus, Patricius, Elpidius, Theophilus, Theodore, Eumathius, Didymion, Ecdicius, Arsenius, Passinicus, Valentinus, Eucarpius, Leontius, Heortasius and Macarius, to their most beloved brothers Ursacius, Valens, Magdonius, Megasius, Germinius, Gaius, Justinus, Optatus, Martialis and the other envoys of the synod of Ariminum: greeting in the Lord.

Since we are striving for unity and true peace, and are resisting heresy by mandate of the synod, we have thought it right to make known to you what is being done concerning the Church, lest ignorance make you partners in so great an impiety. Yet we do not suppose you are unaware that it is not without reason that we, the envoys of the whole synod, that is, of a number of bishops far greater than a hundred, have refrained until now from entering this church.

For this reason we want you also to be informed, so that the heresy which already dominates within the Church may not grow wholly strong: the heresy that has dared to deny that our Lord Jesus Christ is truly the only-begotten Son of God, God from God, like the Father. We want you to know what blasphemous teachings about the only-begotten God these men both hold and preach. We have proved this very thing to the most pious emperor Constantius as well, and, being moved, he most religiously wished all these things to be anathematized. But now a trick is being prepared: that Aetius, the author of this heresy, should be condemned in person rather than these impious sayings, so that the sentence may appear to have been passed against a man rather than against a doctrine. We warn you, therefore, brothers, to examine these things carefully and to take care that the catholic faith may remain. For the rest, your charity has no doubt that everything must be reported to the Western churches just as it is being done. We wish you, brothers, good health in the Lord.
Narrative text.

(2) Once these documents had been received, with the blasphemies mentioned above attached to them, a false charge was brought against the man who had received them. And such fury came over the hypocrites at the exposure of their fraud that they threatened him with deposition. What anguish of a guilty conscience it is to be terrified that anyone should recognize the truth! If this book of Valens and Ursacius does not express your faith, why do you not agree to its condemnation? Is it not agreed among all, by the common assent of the human race, that poison is an evil, that killing the innocent is a crime, and that impiety towards the Lord is a horror? But whoever does not condemn these things when they are brought before him must necessarily declare himself a partner in their endeavor, for there is no one who does not denounce what he hates, and approve what he does not denounce.

For when you came to Constantinople after the synod of Seleucia, why did you immediately join yourselves to condemned heretics, without delaying your approach to them at all, and without allowing yourselves, as prudent counsel would require, any time to make inquiry? Then the envoys of the Eastern synod, who were not in communion with those bishops, came to you, explained all the proceedings, and showed you the heresy that was dominant. Should you not, at least then, have stood aside and kept yourselves as arbiters of all the disputes?

But by some intention of yours, I know not what, you did not accept the judgment of a right conscience. For you at once attached yourselves to your own people and entered into communion with your blasphemies. Nor did you even adopt the counsel of having the synod of Ariminum taken into account, in case shame had misled some [?]. For by not anathematizing your own people you at once betrayed your deceit.

(3) For in an assembly of many who were challenging you as to why you would not also say that the Son of God is not a creature, you answered that at holy Ariminum it was not denied that Christ is a creature, but only that he is like the other creatures. When it was said that "he is not created like the other works", this did not mean, you said, that he is not a creation, but that he is set apart from the others, so that, though entirely unlike the others, he is still not something of another kind. As if any creature were like the others: an angel like a man, a man like a bird, a bird like a beast! If I am lying in this, those who heard you are my witnesses. And if they keep silent, your book, which

you have most impiously defended, speaks on my side: in it the Son is as foreign to the Father, and Christ to God, as glass is to a sapphire. Next, take the point on which you deceived your hearers: that "he is not from things that did not exist, but from God". Even though you said this too, was the pretence not obvious, since according to your profession he is "not from things that did not exist, but from God" only because God's will was the beginning of his coming into being? I am plainly lying if, while the Easterners connived at it through the agreement of their own document,

you did not condemn those who had said that he has what he was born not from the substance but from the will. You also profess that he is "eternal with the Father". You would indeed have spoken truly, had I not been faced with the protest why they had preached that the true only-begotten God was born of God the true Father before eternal times, so that his eternity with the Father would be the eternity of angels

and human souls, an eternity not of what came before but of what is to come. You have also said that he is like the Father "according to the Scriptures", as if according to the Scriptures man too were not like God, and the mustard seed, the leaven and the dragnet like the kingdom of heaven. But it is pointless to run through the lies of your hypocrisy, for the works of your impiety cry out against you.

(4) A slave who is, I will not say good, but at least tolerable, hears an insult to his master unwillingly and, if he is allowed, avenges it. A soldier wards off danger from his king, even by putting his own body in the way and disregarding his life. Even dogs kept to guard the house understand by a kind of natural sense and bark, and when some scent of people approaching reaches them, they rush with all their bounds towards the very thing they suspect. You heard Christ, the true Son of God and only-begotten God, denied; you are thought to (deny) him, and you keep quiet. Why do I say keep quiet? You resist those who protest and join those who raise the clamor. And that is not the half of it: weapons for preaching impiety are even taken from your library, and war is waged against God with your support.

Where, then, is the profession you made at Nike in Thrace, in which you said that all heresies were condemned? Your falsehood has been dragged into the light; the Sun of righteousness has exposed the night of your profession to his preachers. For you approve these things and condemn them, and then go over to the heretics. So what you formerly concealed in order to deceive men, you have now betrayed to the point of openly professing your hatred of Christ, who is God.
